title: Legislative and adjudicative facts
summary: Adjudicative facts concern particular parties and events; legislative facts inform general policy, legal rules, and discretionary judgment.
notes:
Kenneth Culp Davis distinguishes facts about who did what, where, when, how, and why from general information used to choose law or policy. Parties are especially well placed to correct factual assertions about their own conduct, which supports an opportunity to know and answer adverse evidence in adjudication. Agencies and other experts may know more about broader policy facts, for which a trial is often a less useful means of inquiry.

The assigned notes compare that distinction with generality and prospectivity. Neither the number of people affected nor the future operation of a decision supplies a universal answer: class litigation and private legislation complicate the first, while prospective judicial remedies and agency precedents complicate the second. Florida East Coast Railway used the general, prospective policy character of incentive rates in construing a statutory hearing requirement. The resulting classification still must respect the APA’s definitions and any particular congressional procedural command.
